chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Makes a Stock Cyclical or Defensive

lessons.title: Measuring It Yourself: Earnings Volatility, Beta, and Drawdowns on Screener.in

body.text: Stop borrowing labels from TV anchors and fund factsheets. Three numbers, all of which you can pull in fifteen minutes, tell you where a stock sits on the spectrum: how much its earnings swing, how much its price moves with the Nifty, and how far it has fallen before.

children.text: The last two lessons gave you the concept and the five positions on the spectrum. This lesson turns them into a measurement routine. Earnings volatility is the primary evidence because cyclicality lives in the business. Beta and drawdowns are supporting evidence because they show how the market has actually treated the stock. Use all three, and trust earnings when they disagree.

stats.label: Measure 1
stats.context: Primary evidence, from the Profit and Loss table

stats.label: Measure 2
stats.context: How much the price moves with the Nifty 50

children.text: Open any company on Screener.in and scroll to the Profit and Loss section. You get more than a decade of annual Sales, Operating Profit, OPM %, and Net Profit in one table. From that table, pull four numbers.
how many of the last 10 years ended with a net loss.
how many years net profit fell compared with the year before.
the gap between the highest and lowest operating profit margin. A cyclical's margin can move 15 to 25 percentage points across a cycle; a staples company's often stays within a few points.

markDefs.definition: Standard deviation divided by the average. It expresses how widely values are spread relative to their typical size, so companies of different sizes can be compared.

children.text: of 10 years of net profit, which squeezes the whole pattern into one comparable number.

body.latex: \text{CV} = \frac{\text{Standard deviation of annual net profit}}{\text{Average annual net profit}}
body.caption: In Excel or Google Sheets: =STDEV.P(range)/AVERAGE(range)
Worked example: two illustrative companies, net profit in ₹ crore

body.text: The coefficient of variation breaks down when average profit is close to zero or negative. A company that lost money in most years can show a meaningless or negative CV. In those cases, rely on loss years, decline years, and the OPM range instead.

markDefs.definition: A measure of how much a stock's returns tend to move relative to the market index. A beta of 1.3 means the stock has historically moved about 1.3% for every 1% move in the index.

children.text: tells you how sensitive a stock's price has been to the Nifty 50. Cyclicals usually carry a beta above 1, because the market reprices their future profits aggressively whenever the economic outlook changes. Defensives usually sit below 1. Beta is about price behaviour, not earnings, which is why it supports your earnings analysis rather than replacing it.

body.caption: R = periodic returns, usually monthly over 3 to 5 years

children.text: You do not need to do this by hand. Screener.in's company pages focus on financials, so calculate beta yourself in a spreadsheet. Download 3 to 5 years of month-end closing prices for the stock and for the Nifty 50 from the NSE website, turn each into monthly percentage returns, and use =SLOPE(stock returns, Nifty returns). The slope of that regression is beta.

body.title: What Beta Can and Cannot Tell You

columns.label: Useful for
points: Estimating how hard a stock may fall in a broad market sell-off
Comparing price sensitivity across stocks and funds
Checking whether the market already treats a stock as cyclical

columns.label: Misleading when
points: The period is short or unusual, such as a single crash year
A stock is thinly traded, so its price barely moves with anything
Company-specific news, like a merger or USFDA action, dominated the period
The business has changed, so past price behaviour no longer fits

children.text: Drawdown is the fall from a previous peak to the lowest point before a new peak. Maximum drawdown is the worst such fall over the period you study. It answers the question that actually matters when you hold a stock: how much pain has it delivered before? On Screener.in, set the price chart to its longest range and find the biggest peak-to-trough fall. Then compare it with the Nifty 50 over the same window. In 2008, the Nifty 50 fell more than 60% from its January peak to its October low. A stock that fell 80% in the same window was amplifying the cycle; one that fell 30% was cushioning it.

body.caption: Always measure from the peak, never from your own buying price

body.title: Calculate the Drawdown
body.prompt: A capital goods stock hit ₹1,250 at its peak, then fell to ₹700 before recovering. What was its maximum drawdown? Enter the size of the fall as a positive number.
body.explanation: (700 - 1,250) / 1,250 × 100 = -44%. Note the recovery math too: to get from ₹700 back to ₹1,250, the stock needs to rise about 78.6%. Deep drawdowns take far larger gains to repair, which is why cyclical drawdowns can trap investors for years.

body.title: For Python users: beta and maximum drawdown in a few lines

children.text: If you export daily closing prices for a stock and the Nifty 50 as CSV files with Date and Close columns, this script calculates both measures. Rename the columns first if your download uses different headers.

content.code:
import pandas as pd

stock = pd.read_csv("stock.csv", parse_dates=["Date"], index_col="Date")["Close"]
nifty = pd.read_csv("nifty50.csv", parse_dates=["Date"], index_col="Date")["Close"]

prices = pd.concat([stock, nifty], axis=1, keys=["stock", "nifty"]).dropna().sort_index()

# Beta from month-end returns (use "M" instead of "ME" on pandas older than 2.2)
monthly = prices.resample("ME").last().pct_change().dropna()
beta = monthly["stock"].cov(monthly["nifty"]) / monthly["nifty"].var()

# Maximum drawdown from daily prices
drawdown = prices["stock"] / prices["stock"].cummax() - 1

print(f"Beta: {beta:.2f}")
print(f"Maximum drawdown: {drawdown.min():.1%}")
content.caption: Beta from monthly returns, maximum drawdown from daily prices

body.title: When the Measures Disagree
body.question: A company has zero loss years, a profit CV of 0.18, and an OPM range of 3 percentage points over 10 years. But its beta is 1.3 and it fell more than the Nifty 50 in the last correction. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: It is a cyclical, because beta and drawdown are the market's verdict
It is a defensive business whose stock has recently traded with high sentiment or valuation risk
The data is contradictory, so the stock cannot be classified
It is a deep cyclical in disguise
body.explanation: Earnings are the primary evidence, and every earnings measure here says defensive. A high beta and deep fall usually point to something else: an expensive valuation that derated, heavy institutional flows, or company-specific worries. The business is defensive; the stock carried price risk.

body.title: Your 15-Minute Measurement Routine
steps: Open the company on Screener.in and go to the Profit and Loss table
Count loss years and profit decline years over the last 10 years
Note the highest and lowest OPM % and calculate the range
Use Export to Excel, or copy the Net Profit row into a sheet, and calculate =STDEV.P(range)/AVERAGE(range)
Download 3 to 5 years of monthly closes for the stock and the Nifty 50 from the NSE website and calculate beta with =SLOPE()
Check the longest price chart for the maximum drawdown and compare it with the Nifty 50's fall in the same period
Score each measure on the scorecard and place the stock on the spectrum, giving earnings measures the most weight

body.label: NSE India
body.description: Historical price data for individual stocks and for indices like the Nifty 50, which you need for beta and drawdown calculations.

points: Earnings volatility is the primary evidence: count loss years and decline years, check the OPM range, and calculate the coefficient of variation of net profit
Beta measures how much the price moves with the Nifty 50; cyclicals usually sit above 1.2 and defensives below 0.8
Maximum drawdown shows the worst historical price pain; compare it with the index in the same bear market
Deep drawdowns need much larger gains to recover: a 44% fall needs a 78.6% rise to get back to the peak
When measures disagree, trust earnings for the business and treat beta and drawdown as signals of price or valuation risk
